mcqs.question: Are https://app.example.com and https://api.example.com the same origin?
options: Yes, because they share the same registrable parent domain, example.com
No, because the host differs, even though the scheme and effective port match
Yes, since only the scheme and port need to match for two URLs to be same-origin
It depends on whether both are served over HTTPS
mcqs.explanation: Origin equality requires scheme, host, and port to all match — subdomains count as different hosts, so sharing a parent domain grants nothing automatically. This surprises people specifically because it feels like they should be related.

mcqs.question: A malicious page's script issues a fetch to your-bank.com while you're logged in there in another tab. What does the Same-Origin Policy actually prevent here?
options: It prevents the request from ever being sent to your-bank.com at all
It prevents your bank's session cookies from ever being attached to any cross-site request
It prevents the malicious script from reading the response, even though the request may still be sent and succeed server-side
It automatically logs the user out of your-bank.com the moment it detects the cross-origin attempt
mcqs.explanation: SOP's guarantee is specifically about response readability, not request sending — the request can still go out with cookies attached, which is exactly the gap CSRF exploits. SOP just stops the attacker's script from seeing what came back.

mcqs.question: In the CORS preflight handshake, what does the OPTIONS request check before the real request is sent?
options: Whether the user has a valid session cookie for the target origin
Whether the server's TLS certificate is valid for the target origin
Whether the server permits this specific origin, method, and headers, via Access-Control-Allow-* response headers
Whether the DNS record for the target host resolves correctly
mcqs.explanation: The preflight is purely a permission check against the server's declared CORS policy for that origin/method/header combination — it has nothing to do with cookies, TLS validity, or DNS, which are all resolved independently.

mcqs.question: A cross-origin fetch is made with credentials: 'include'. Which server-side response combination is required for the browser to expose the response to your JavaScript?
options: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Allow-Origin set to the exact requesting origin, plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Only Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is required; the origin header is optional
Access-Control-Allow-Methods listing every HTTP method, regardless of the requesting origin
mcqs.explanation: Credentialed requests require both an exact, non-wildcard origin match and the explicit credentials flag — the browser enforces this pairing itself and won't proceed with a wildcard origin no matter what else the server sends.

mcqs.question: A fetch call fails in the console with a CORS error, but the Network tab shows the request completed with a 200 status and a real response body. What does that combination tell you?
options: The server never received the request at all
The response was corrupted in transit due to a network error
The request was blocked by an ad blocker extension, unrelated to CORS
The browser received a valid response but refused to expose it to your JavaScript because the CORS headers didn't permit your origin
mcqs.explanation: A completed request with data in the Network tab plus a console CORS error is the classic signature of the browser blocking JS-side access to an otherwise-successful response — it's a header mismatch, not a network or server failure.

mcqs.question: A server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * and the client sends the request with credentials: 'include'. What happens?
options: The browser accepts it, assuming Access-Control-Allow-Credentials was also likely set to true
The request succeeds but the browser silently strips the cookies before sending
The browser refuses to expose the response, since a wildcard origin is disallowed whenever credentials are involved — enforced regardless of server intent
The server automatically downgrades the request to a non-credentialed one
mcqs.explanation: This combination is blocked by the browser itself as a fetch-spec rule, not a configurable server behavior — a wildcard origin plus credentials would let any site read cookie-authenticated responses, so browsers refuse it unconditionally.
